label: GDSII records and stream structure
prereqs: Writing a number in another base
lesson:
# GDSII records and stream structure

Physical verification starts from the layout stream that will become masks. GDSII, the oldest and most widely exchanged stream format, is a flat sequence of binary records that describe libraries, structures (cells) and the elements inside them. A verification tool reads nothing else: no nets, no device types, only layers, numbers and coordinates. Knowing exactly what the records hold tells a tool designer what must be reconstructed later (connectivity, devices) and what the file size and parse cost will be.

## Records and element sizes

Every GDSII record starts with a 4-byte header: a 2-byte total length, a 1-byte record type and a 1-byte data type. A polygon is a BOUNDARY element written as five records: BOUNDARY (header only, 4 bytes), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each, 6 bytes each), XY (4-byte x and y integers per point) and ENDEL (4 bytes). The XY list closes the ring by repeating the first vertex, so a polygon with $n$ vertices stores $n + 1$ points and costs $4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n+1)) + 4 = 32 + 8n$ bytes. A rectangle ($n = 4$) is 64 bytes. A PATH element (a wire given by its centerline) adds a WIDTH record (8 bytes) and does not close its point list, so $m$ points cost $32 + 8m$ bytes. Layers and datatypes are only numbers: the meaning of layer 68, datatype 20 lives in the technology's layer map, not in the file.

## Counting records in a structure

A structure is framed by BGNSTR, STRNAME and ENDSTR: three records around its elements. A BOUNDARY contributes 5 records, an SREF (a placement of another structure) 4 records (SREF, SNAME, XY, ENDEL), and a TEXT label 6 (TEXT, LAYER, TEXTTYPE, XY, STRING, ENDEL), ignoring optional records such as STRANS for rotation or mirroring. A structure with 19 boundaries, 2 SREFs and 4 labels therefore has $3 + 5 \cdot 19 + 4 \cdot 2 + 6 \cdot 4 = 130$ records. A reader is a loop over records with a state machine that knows which records may follow which. Text labels matter more than their size suggests: they are the only way a stream carries net and pin names, and LVS depends on them.

## The byte size of a structure

BGNSTR carries twelve 2-byte integers (modification and access dates), so it is 28 bytes. STRNAME and SNAME carry an ASCII name padded with a null byte to an even length. A structure INV with 3 rectangles and 2 SREFs of ADC_BIAS costs $28 + (4 + 4) + 3 \cdot 64 + 2 \cdot (4 + (4 + 8) + 12 + 4) + 4 = 296$ bytes: the name INV pads to 4 bytes and ADC_BIAS is already even at 8. These fixed costs explain why flat GDSII files of large designs reach many gigabytes: every rectangle pays 64 bytes, and nothing is shared between records. They also make GDSII trivially seekable and easy to parse in a streaming pass, which is one reason it survives.

## Going deeper

The Calma "GDSII Stream Format Manual" (Release 6.0); the KLayout documentation on stream formats.

How many bytes does a polygon with 6 vertices occupy?

label: GDSII and OASIS
prereqs: Writing a number in another base
lesson:
# GDSII and OASIS

OASIS is the newer stream format designed to replace GDSII for very large layouts, especially post-OPC mask data. Both describe the same thing: cells, placements, polygons on numbered layers. OASIS is typically several to many times smaller because it removes the redundancy that GDSII writes into every record. For a verification tool, the format decides parse cost, memory, and how much repetition the reader can recover without analysis.

## Variable-length integers

GDSII writes every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer. OASIS writes unsigned integers in 7-bit groups, one group per byte, with the top bit set when another byte follows. A value $v$ with $b$ significant bits takes $\lceil b / 7 \rceil$ bytes, so 100 takes one byte, 1266 (11 bits) two bytes, and 300000 (19 bits) three bytes. Signed integers spend one bit of the first byte on the sign. Because OASIS can also write a vertex as a delta from the previous one, most coordinates in a dense layout are small numbers and cost one or two bytes. The same idea, varint encoding, appears in many binary formats; here it is the single largest source of savings on uncompressed data.

## Storing a regular array

Repetition is the second lever. In GDSII, a $16 \times 22$ via array can be written as 352 flat rectangles at 64 bytes each (22528 bytes), as 352 SREFs of a one-rectangle cell, or as one AREF. The AREF costs AREF 4 + SNAME + COLROW 8 + XY 28 + ENDEL 4 bytes; its XY holds three points (origin, column end, row end). With the five-letter name FILL1 padded to 6, the cell costs $28 + 10 + 64 + 4 = 106$ bytes and the AREF $4 + 10 + 8 + 28 + 4 = 54$, so 160 bytes in total. GDSII can only express repetition of placements, and only as one regular two-dimensional array. OASIS attaches repetitions to placements and to individual shapes, with regular and irregular forms.

## Why OASIS files are smaller

Four mechanisms combine. Variable-length integers and relative coordinates shrink numbers. Modal variables let a record omit fields equal to the previous record's (layer, datatype, width, geometry size): an info byte says which fields are present. Repetitions turn arrays of identical shapes into one record. Name tables store each cell name and text string once and refer to it by index. OASIS also defines optional compressed blocks (CBLOCK, using DEFLATE). None of this changes the geometry, so a converter between the formats is lossless for the shared feature set. GDSII remains common because every tool reads it and its fixed records are simple; OASIS dominates where size hurts most, such as post-OPC data headed to the mask shop.

## Going deeper

SEMI P39, the OASIS specification; the KLayout documentation on OASIS reading and writing.

A) 2 bytes

B) 3 bytes

C) 4 bytes

A) Support for more than one layer

B) The ability to store hierarchy

C) The fixed 4-byte integer width of coordinates and sizes

D) The ability to store text labels

label: Database units and the manufacturing grid
lesson:
# Database units and the manufacturing grid

Layout databases store integers, not lengths. The stream's UNITS record says how long one database unit (DBU) is, and every coordinate counts those units. Integer coordinates make Boolean operations and spacing checks exact and reproducible, which a signoff tool needs. Two limits follow: the finite integer width caps the coordinate range, and the foundry's manufacturing grid restricts which integers are legal vertex positions.

## Database units

GDSII's UNITS record holds two 8-byte reals: the size of a database unit in user units (often 0.001, meaning micrometres) and in metres (often $10^{-9}$, meaning 1 nm). A coordinate in micrometres becomes an integer by multiplying by DBUs per micrometre. With a 0.5 nm unit there are 2000 DBU per um, so $x = 213.43$ um is stored as 426860. Converting a design to a finer unit multiplies every coordinate exactly; converting to a coarser unit needs rounding and can move edges, which is why mixing IP with different units is a classic source of off-grid errors.

## The coordinate range

GDSII coordinates are signed 32-bit integers, so the largest value is $2^{31} - 1 = 2147483647$ DBU. With a 1 nm unit that is about 2147.48 mm, far larger than any die. With a 0.1 nm unit it is 214.75 mm, still enough for a wafer-scale layout but no longer generous. Inside a tool, products of coordinates (areas, cross products in orientation tests) need twice the bits, so engines either use 64-bit intermediates or restrict the range. Choosing the unit is a technology decision made once, because it fixes both precision and reach.

## The manufacturing grid

Foundries require every vertex to lie on a manufacturing grid, for example 5 nm, so that mask writers and OPC work on a common lattice. A vertex is legal only if both coordinates are multiples of the grid; being an integer DBU is not enough. With a 10 nm grid, $(3050, 190)$ passes, while $(163, 2120)$ and $(1310, 1053)$ fail. Off-grid vertices usually come from scaling, rotation by non-right angles, mirroring about a half-unit line, or Boolean results of diagonal edges. A grid check is cheap (a divisibility test per vertex) and runs early, because off-grid geometry corrupts the precise checks that follow.

problems.e: One um is 4000 database units of 0.25 nm, so 60.08525 um is 60.08525 x 4000 = 240341.

label: Hierarchy with SREF and AREF
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Hierarchy with SREF and AREF

A layout is a directed acyclic graph of cells: a cell holds shapes and placements of other cells. GDSII expresses placements as SREF (one instance) and AREF (a regular array). Hierarchy is compression: a bit cell stored once may appear a million times. Every verification engine must decide what to flatten and what to keep, and that decision starts with counting what the hierarchy expands to.

## Flattening a cell tree

Flattening replaces each placement by a transformed copy of the placed cell's contents, recursively. Counts compose bottom-up. If LEAF holds 25 shapes, MID holds 11 shapes and 9 SREFs of LEAF, and TOP holds 4 shapes, 10 SREFs of MID and an AREF of LEAF with 7 columns and 14 rows, then MID expands to $11 + 9 \cdot 25 = 236$ shapes and TOP to $4 + 10 \cdot 236 + 98 \cdot 25 = 4814$. The hierarchy stores only $25 + 11 + 4 = 40$ shapes. A post-order traversal of the cell DAG computes every cell's flat count once, in time linear in the number of cells and placements.

## Placements as paths in the cell DAG

Each flat occurrence of a cell corresponds to one path from the top cell to it in the cell DAG, with edges weighted by instance counts. In the example, LEAF appears $10 \cdot 9 = 90$ times through MID and $7 \cdot 14 = 98$ times through the AREF, 188 placements in all. The count is a sum over paths of the product of edge weights, the same computation as counting paths in a DAG. It is what a flat DRC run pays for each LEAF-level check, and what a hierarchical run can avoid when contexts repeat.

## AREF versus SREF

An SREF costs SREF 4 + SNAME (4 plus the padded name) + XY 12 + ENDEL 4 bytes. An AREF costs AREF 4 + SNAME + COLROW 8 + XY 28 + ENDEL 4 bytes, independent of the array size. For DFFR (4 characters) placed in a $17 \times 22$ grid, 374 SREFs cost $374 \cdot 28 = 10472$ bytes while one AREF costs 52, saving 10420. AREFs also tell a tool that the placements are regular, which a hierarchical engine can exploit: interior instances share one context. The cost is rigidity: an AREF must be a perfect lattice, so one displaced instance breaks it into pieces.

label: Design rule types
prereqs: Database units and the manufacturing grid
lesson:
# Design rule types

Design rules are the foundry's contract with the designer: if every rule passes, the layout is manufacturable with acceptable yield. A rule deck holds thousands of them, but they fall into a small set of types. A DRC engine designer needs that taxonomy because each type maps to a different geometric computation: single-shape measurements, relations between two layers, or checks that depend on context such as connectivity or a window.

## Single-layer rules

Single-layer rules measure one layer. Minimum width is the distance between a shape's own opposite edges; minimum spacing is the distance between facing edges of different shapes; a notch is spacing between facing edges of the same polygon; minimum area bounds the area of each polygon, so small islands (via landing pads) do not lift off. For example, with a 40 nm width rule a 38 nm wire fails, and with a 32 nm spacing rule two wires 30 nm apart fail. All of these operate on the merged layer, after overlapping shapes are combined, and they reduce to edge-pair distance tests or polygon area computations.

## Two-layer rules

Two-layer rules relate shapes on different layers. Enclosure requires an outer layer to surround an inner one by a margin, such as metal around a via cut. Extension requires one layer to continue past another's edge, such as poly past diffusion so the gate end does not shrink (the endcap). Inter-layer spacing keeps, for instance, a contact away from a neighbouring gate. Cut layers have their own spacing and size rules. Engines implement these with Boolean operations and sizing: an enclosure check is a test that the inner layer, grown by the margin, stays inside the outer one.

## Context-dependent rules

Some rules depend on more than local geometry. End-of-line spacing applies more spacing in front of narrow wire ends, because line ends print short and round. Width- and run-length-dependent spacing raises spacing for wide wires that run side by side. Density rules constrain the metal fraction in every window of a given size, which no single shape determines. Antenna rules depend on which metal is electrically connected to a gate at an intermediate manufacturing step, so the engine needs connectivity, not just geometry. These are the expensive checks, and they are where engines differ most.

## Going deeper

A foundry design rule manual for an open PDK, such as the SkyWater SKY130 or GF180MCU documentation.

lesson:
# Width and spacing checks

Width and spacing are the bulk of any rule deck and the first checks an engine must get exactly right. Both are distance computations on rectilinear shapes, but the details matter: which metric, whether corners count, and how the required value changes with the shapes involved. A signoff checker must report every violation and nothing else, so these definitions are exact, not approximate.

## Width violations

For a rectangle, width is the shorter side; for a general polygon it is the smallest distance between opposite edges facing inward. With a 50 nm width rule, a wire $[92, 129] \times [0, 575]$ (37 nm wide) fails and $[67, 445] \times [400, 464]$ (64 nm) passes, however long they are. Width must be measured on the merged layer: two overlapping 30 nm rectangles can form one legal 60 nm wire, while a single legal shape can have a narrow neck. Polygon engines find width violations as pairs of inward-facing edges closer than the rule.

## Euclidean spacing

Spacing between two disjoint rectangles is computed from the gaps of their projections. Let $g_x$ and $g_y$ be the x and y gaps, zero where the projections overlap. The Euclidean distance is $\sqrt{g_x^2 + g_y^2}$: if the projections overlap on one axis, the closest points face each other and the distance is the other gap; otherwise two corners are closest. With a 23 nm rule, shapes with gaps 10 and 15 nm are $\sqrt{325} \approx 18.0$ nm apart and violate, while gaps 20 and 15 give 25 nm and pass. Comparing squared distances with $S^2$ keeps the test in integers.

## Width-dependent spacing

Wide wires need more spacing, for lithography and for reliability. A typical rule is a table: 40 nm normally, 80 nm when either wire is at least 200 nm wide. Each pair's required spacing is looked up from the widths before the distance comparison. For parallel vertical wires, checking neighbours suffices when every wire is at least as wide as the largest rule value: anything farther away is separated by a whole wire. In the general case an engine expands each wide wire by the larger value and queries neighbours, so the table changes the search radius as well as the threshold.

label: Enclosure and extension rules
lesson:
# Enclosure and extension rules

Enclosure and extension rules relate two layers. They keep a via cut inside the metal it lands on despite misalignment, and keep a poly gate long enough past diffusion that the transistor does not leak at its ends. They are computed with Boolean operations and sizing, and modern processes make them direction-dependent, which turns a simple margin test into a small logical condition.

## Enclosure

The enclosure of a via by metal is the smallest distance from a via edge to the corresponding metal edge. For a via $[115, 185] \times [190, 260]$ inside metal $[100, 207] \times [179, 275]$ the margins are left 15, right 22, bottom 11 and top 15 nm, so the enclosure is 11 nm. A negative margin means the via sticks out. Engines check enclosure by sizing: grow the via by the required margin $e$ and test whether the grown shape lies inside the metal, that is, whether (VIA SIZED BY $e$) NOT METAL is empty.

## Two-sided enclosure rules

At advanced nodes enclosure is often asymmetric: the via needs a large margin $b$ on both sides along one axis and only a small margin $a$ along the other, in either orientation. A via with enclosures (left, right, bottom, top) = (35, 33, 33, 11) and the rule $b = 30$, $a = 4$ passes: the horizontal pair gives min 33 at least 30, and the vertical pair min 11 at least 4. A via with (18, 32, 33, 27) fails both orientations. Such rules let line-end metal stop close to a via in the direction of the wire while protecting the sides, and the check becomes min-over-pairs plus an OR of two conditions.

## Extension and endcaps

Extension measures how far one layer continues beyond another. Poly must extend past diffusion at both ends of a gate by the endcap rule $E$, because line-end shortening and rounding would otherwise leave the channel partly ungated. With $E = 110$ nm, a gate whose poly runs from 296 to 857 over diffusion from 370 to 730 has extensions 74 and 127 nm, so its bottom end needs 36 nm more. Repairing short endcaps is a common automated fix, and the total added length tells how much area the fix costs.

lesson:
# Notch, end-of-line and run-length rules

Simple spacing rules treat every pair of facing edges alike. Real decks do not. Edges of the same polygon, wire ends, and long parallel runs of wide wires all have their own rules, because lithography and etch treat them differently. Each variant changes which edge pairs an engine must find and which threshold applies, and they are where many router-produced violations come from.

## Notches

A notch is a gap between two edges of the same polygon that face each other, such as the space between two prongs of a comb. Because the edges belong to one merged polygon, a check that only compares different shapes misses it. For a comb whose prongs span $[0, 130]$, $[160, 290]$ and $[370, 500]$ with a 60 nm notch rule, the first gap (30 nm) violates and the second (80 nm) passes. Engines handle notches by running the spacing search over all edge pairs of the merged layer, including pairs inside one polygon, while skipping adjacent edges that meet at a vertex.

## End-of-line spacing

A wire end narrower than a threshold $W_{eol}$ is a line end. Line ends print shorter than drawn, so they need more spacing in front of them, $S_{eol}$, than the normal spacing $S$. A wire end violates if it is narrow and closer than $S_{eol}$, or closer than $S$ regardless of width. With $S = 40$, $W_{eol} = 60$ and $S_{eol} = 80$ nm, an end 50 nm wide with a 70 nm gap violates, while an end 90 nm wide with the same gap passes. Engines identify line-end edges by their length and their two convex corners, then search a region in front of them.

## Parallel-run-length tables

Spacing tables index the required spacing by the wider wire's width and the length over which the two wires run in parallel. A two-entry example: 40 nm normally, 90 nm when the wider wire is at least 240 nm wide and the parallel run exceeds 500 nm. A pair with width 330, run 850 and spacing 65 needs 90 and fails; a pair with width 390, run 100 and spacing 55 needs only 40 and passes. Computing parallel run length requires the overlap of the two edges' projections, so a table rule needs more than a distance query: it needs the facing edges themselves.

label: Minimum area and via rules
lesson:
# Minimum area and via rules

Area and via rules are where routers most often produce violations: short wire stubs are too small, and wide wires need more than one via cut. These rules also tie verification to yield, because a single via cut is one of the most failure-prone features in a chip. The computations are small, but they recur on millions of connections.

## Minimum area

Minimum area bounds the area of every merged polygon on a layer. A metal stub 50 nm wide and 122 nm long has area 6100 square nm; with an 8000 square nm rule it needs a length of $\lceil 8000 / 50 \rceil = 160$ nm, so 38 nm more. Routers fix area violations by extending a wire end along its direction, which can in turn create a new spacing violation in front of it. Minimum enclosed area (for holes) is the dual rule. Because area is a property of the merged polygon, two short stubs that touch can pass together while each would fail alone.

## Fitting a via array

Where two wide wires overlap, a via array connects them. With cuts of size $v$, cut spacing $s$ and enclosure $e$, the usable length along x is $W - 2e$, and $n$ cuts need $nv + (n - 1)s$, so $n = \lfloor (W - 2e + s) / (v + s) \rfloor$. For a 313 by 480 nm overlap with $v = 50$, $s = 50$ and $e = 30$: $\lfloor 303 / 100 \rfloor = 3$ columns and $\lfloor 470 / 100 \rfloor = 4$ rows, 12 cuts. Real decks add rules for cut arrays (larger spacing inside big arrays), so generators must follow the deck, not this formula alone.

## Minimum-cut rules

A wide wire carries more current and its via is a larger reliability risk, so decks require multiple cuts when a via lands on a wide wire: for example 2 cuts at widths of at least 250 nm and 4 cuts at widths of at least 740 nm. A connection with width 600 nm and 1 cut fails; one with width 690 nm and 3 cuts passes. Separately, DFM flows add redundant cuts wherever space allows, even where the rule does not demand them. The rule check needs the via's connectivity to both wires and their widths, which is why it is implemented on derived layers that combine cut and metal information.

label: How a DRC engine works
lesson:
# How a DRC engine works

A DRC engine turns a rule deck and a layout into a list of violations. Its core is a small set of geometric primitives (merging, Boolean operations, sizing, edge-pair distance queries) driven by spatial data structures so that each shape is compared only with nearby shapes. Engine designers trade between edge-based and polygon-based formulations and between batch and incremental use.

## Candidate pairs and spatial filtering

Comparing every pair of $n$ shapes costs $n(n-1)/2$ tests, impossible for billions of shapes. Engines first find candidate pairs whose bounding boxes, one expanded by the rule distance $S$, overlap: both the x gap and the y gap are below $S$. Only candidates get the exact Euclidean test. For six shapes there are 15 pairs; perhaps 4 survive the box filter, and the exact test confirms some of those, since a diagonal pair with gaps 15 and 15 nm passes the filter for $S = 20$ but is 21.2 nm apart. Spatial indexes (R-trees, grids) or a plane sweep find candidates in near-linear time.

## Polygon-based checks by sizing

A polygon-based engine expresses rules as Boolean algebra on layers. A spacing check can be written as: grow every shape by $S/2$ and report where grown shapes of different polygons overlap. For shapes facing across a gap $g$ with y overlap $o_y$, the marker is $(S - g)$ by $(o_y + S)$, because the growth also extends the shapes' ends. With $S = 24$, $g = 5$ and $o_y = 14$, the marker area is $19 \cdot 38 = 722$ square nm. Square growth measures the Chebyshev metric, so engines that need Euclidean spacing round corners or switch to edge-pair tests near corners.

## Edge-based and polygon-based engines

Edge-based engines, such as Magic's, express each rule as a relation between edges: for an edge of layer A, look outward a distance $d$ for edges of a forbidden layer. They are natural for incremental checking while editing. Polygon-based engines, such as the Boolean pipelines in KLayout and commercial signoff tools, build derived layers and run measurements on them, which suits rule decks with many layer combinations. Both need merged geometry, exact integer predicates and a halo when the die is cut into tiles for parallel work. Results come back as edge pairs or small marker polygons tagged with the rule name, which downstream tools and agents consume.

## Going deeper

The KLayout DRC reference manual; Ousterhout, "Corner Stitching: A Data-Structuring Technique for VLSI Layout Tools" (IEEE TCAD, 1984).

lesson:
# Sweep-line spacing checks

Batch DRC engines process a layer with a sweep: a vertical line moves across the die, and only shapes near the line are compared. The sweep turns a quadratic all-pairs problem into one whose cost grows with the number of shapes and the number of near pairs. Its data structures, an event queue in x and an interval structure in y, are the heart of many checkers and Boolean engines.

## The active set

In a spacing sweep for rule $S$, a shape enters the active set at its left edge $x_1$ and leaves at $x_2 + S$, so it is still present when any shape starting within the rule distance arrives. The active set at a sweep position is the set of intervals $[x_1, x_2 + S]$ containing it. Its maximum size bounds memory and the work per event. Shapes $[46, 78]$ and $[28, 68]$ with $S = 27$ are active on $[46, 105]$ and $[28, 95]$, so both are active at $x = 60$. The maximum is found by scanning event points in order, adding at left events and removing at right events.

## Querying the active set

When a shape arrives, the engine asks which active shapes come closer than $S$ in y, that is, which y-intervals $[a, b]$ satisfy $a < y_2 + S$ and $b > y_1 - S$. An interval tree or a balanced tree of y-intervals answers this in $O(\log n + k)$ time for $k$ results. For a new shape on $[133, 154]$ with $S = 14$, the active interval $[105, 119]$ fails ($119 < 119$ is false) while $[94, 131]$ is returned. Only returned shapes get the exact distance test. The query window is the shape's y-extent grown by the rule distance.

## What the sweep saves

Brute force compares $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. The sweep compares only pairs near in both x and y, which in real layouts is roughly linear in $n$ because each shape has a bounded number of neighbours. For six scattered shapes, all 15 pairs may be far apart, and the sweep then makes no exact tests at all. The total cost is $O(n \log n + k)$ for $n$ shapes and $k$ near pairs. The same sweep structure computes Boolean operations and union areas, so one well-engineered sweep kernel serves many checks.

## Going deeper

de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld and Overmars, "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (3rd ed.), chapters on line-segment intersection and interval trees.

label: Hierarchical DRC
lesson:
# Hierarchical DRC

A modern chip repeats a few thousand cells billions of times. Hierarchical DRC checks each cell once and reuses the result wherever the surroundings are the same, checking only the regions where instances interact. Done well, it cuts runtime and memory by orders of magnitude; done naively, it reports false errors or misses real ones. The central difficulty is the context problem.

## Reporting errors once per cell

A flat run sees every copy of every shape, so an error inside a cell is reported once per placement. If cell A has 5 internal violations and is placed 47 times, cell B has 5 and is placed 30 times, and the top cell adds 6, a flat run reports $5 \cdot 47 + 5 \cdot 30 + 6 = 391$ violations. A hierarchical run reports each cell's errors once, in the cell's coordinates: $5 + 5 + 6 = 16$. The smaller report is also the more useful one, because one edit to the cell master fixes all placements, provided the error does not depend on context.

## Interaction regions between instances

Instances interact where their shapes come within the largest rule distance of each other. In an array of cells with metal along all four boundary edges, horizontal neighbours interact if the x gap between cells is below the spacing rule $S$, vertical neighbours if the y gap is, and diagonal neighbours if $\sqrt{g_x^2 + g_y^2} < S$. A $c \times r$ array has $(c-1)r$ horizontal, $c(r-1)$ vertical and $2(c-1)(r-1)$ diagonal neighbour pairs. Each interacting pair is a region the engine checks with shapes from both instances. Regular arrays produce few distinct interaction types, which the engine checks once each.

## The context problem

A cell clean in isolation can violate a rule in context: a top-level wire passes 20 nm from a cell shape, or two overlapping instances bring shapes together. The engine must therefore check each instance's boundary region together with its surroundings. When placements see different surroundings, engines create variants of the cell or process interaction regions separately. Hierarchy pays off when cells interact only through thin boundary regions; layouts with many overlaps or tiny cells placed once gain nothing and can run slower than flat. KLayout's deep mode and commercial hierarchical engines differ mainly in how they manage contexts.

label: Rule decks and derived layers
lesson:
# Rule decks and derived layers

A rule deck is a program. It names the stream's layers, derives new layers by Boolean and sizing operations, and runs checks on them, each tagged with a rule name. Most of a deck's complexity sits in derived layers that express the physical objects a rule talks about: gates, source and drain, wide metal, via landings. Engine designers optimize deck execution as a dataflow graph of layer operations.

## Derived layers by Boolean operations

Derived layers come from AND, OR, NOT and XOR of drawn layers. GATE = POLY AND ACTIVE is the transistor channel; SD = ACTIVE NOT POLY the source and drain; FIELDPOLY = POLY NOT ACTIVE the poly used as wire. For POLY $[54, 71] \times [11, 134]$ and ACTIVE $[38, 150] \times [44, 99]$, GATE is $[54, 71] \times [44, 99]$ with area 935 square nm, and SD has area $112 \cdot 55 - 935 = 5225$. A rule written on GATE fires only on channels, not on poly wiring, which is the point of deriving it.

## Sizing inside a deck

Sizing grows or shrinks every shape by a distance, and decks combine it with Booleans. HALO = (M1 SIZED BY 15) AND M2 finds metal 2 within 15 nm of metal 1. For M1 $[23, 81] \times [2, 52]$ grown to $[8, 96] \times [-13, 67]$ and M2 $[3, 63] \times [45, 72]$, HALO is $[8, 63] \times [45, 67]$, area 1210, while the unsized overlap is only 280. Sizing down then up (an opening) removes features narrower than twice the distance, which is how decks find narrow necks and slivers.

## What a rule deck is

A deck contains layer definitions (stream layer and datatype to name), derived-layer operations, check statements with rule names and thresholds, and switches for process options. It is written in the language of one tool (Calibre's SVRF, KLayout's Ruby-based DSL, Magic's technology file), so a foundry maintains one deck per supported tool and qualifies each against test layouts. Rule names key everything downstream: reports, waivers, and automated fix strategies. The engine executes the deck as a graph: shared derived layers are computed once and freed after last use, and independent checks run in parallel.

## Going deeper

The KLayout DRC reference manual; the DRC decks distributed with the SkyWater SKY130 open PDK.

# Device recognition from layer Booleans

LVS compares the circuit drawn in the layout with the schematic. The layout has no devices, only shapes, so the first step is recognizing devices from layer combinations: a transistor is wherever poly crosses diffusion, typed by the well and implant layers around it, with W and L measured from the gate region. Recognition is a set of derived-layer rules in the LVS deck, and every later step depends on getting it exactly right.

## Gates from poly and diffusion

The gate layer is GATE = POLY AND DIFF. Each connected piece of it is one transistor channel, and the diffusion on its two sides becomes source and drain. A vertical poly line that crosses two diffusion rows inside their x-ranges forms two transistors, one per row, while a poly line passing beside a row forms none there. A poly line that only partly overlaps a diffusion edge makes a malformed device, which the deck flags. Counting gates is counting connected components of the GATE layer, and splitting diffusion by GATE is what separates the source and drain terminals.

## Channel width and length

For a gate region, L is measured along the direction of current flow, across the poly line, and W along the poly, across the diffusion. For a vertical poly $[34, 64] \times [-66, 984]$ crossing diffusion $[0, 240] \times [0, 920]$, the gate is $[34, 64] \times [0, 920]$, so L = 30 nm and W = 920 nm. Rotating the layout swaps which coordinate gives W, so extractors measure from the edges where gate meets diffusion (their total length is 2W for a rectangular gate) rather than from x or y. Non-rectangular gates, such as bent poly, need W and L formulas defined by the deck.

## Device types from wells and implants

The device type comes from the layers around the gate. In a p-substrate process, a gate whose channel lies inside NWELL with p-plus implant is a PMOS; outside the well with n-plus implant it is an NMOS. Thick-oxide, low-threshold and other variants are recognized by additional marker layers. If a well or implant is missing or misdrawn, the device is recognized as a different type or not at all, and LVS later reports a type mismatch even though the poly and diffusion are perfect. Recognition rules therefore encode the process's device catalogue.

# Layout netlist extraction

After devices are recognized, the extractor builds the nets: which shapes are electrically connected through overlaps and vias. The result is a netlist of devices and nets that LVS compares with the schematic. Extraction is a connected-components problem over a huge geometric graph, and its mistakes, real or false, are what LVS reports as shorts and opens.

## Connectivity by union-find

The deck declares which layers connect: shapes on the same conducting layer connect where they overlap or touch, and a via connects the shapes above and below it that contain it. Crossing without a via does not connect. The extractor runs union-find over shapes: one union per overlapping same-layer pair (found by a sweep) and one per via. The number of disjoint sets is the number of nets. Seven wire shapes with three vias may collapse into three nets. Union-find with path compression runs in nearly linear time, so connectivity is cheap compared with finding the overlaps.

## Labels, shorts and net names

Text labels attach names to the shapes they sit on. After extraction, each net collects the names of the labels on it. A net carrying two different names, such as A and Y, is reported as a short: somewhere shapes that should be separate are connected. A schematic net whose name appears on two different layout nets suggests an open. The same name repeated on one net is fine. Label attachment follows the deck's rules for text layers, so a label on the wrong text layer names nothing.

## Critical vias and opens

A via is critical if removing it alone splits a net: it is a bridge of the connectivity graph. Removing a critical via creates an open, while a via with a parallel path through other shapes can fail without changing the netlist. Counting critical vias is a bridge computation: remove each via, recount components, or use a linear-time bridge-finding search. The same analysis motivates redundant vias for yield and explains how a single missing via in a large net shows up in LVS as one schematic net matched to two layout nets.

lesson:
# Device reduction and property comparison

Layouts draw devices differently from schematics: one schematic transistor becomes four parallel fingers, a resistor becomes a serpentine of segments. Before comparison, LVS reduces the layout netlist to logical devices by merging parallel (and optionally series) devices, then compares device properties against tolerances. These steps decide whether a correct layout matches at all.

## Parallel merging

Devices are merged in parallel when they have the same type, the same gate net, the same pair of source and drain nets in either order, and the same L. The merged device's W is the sum. A list of nine layout transistors might reduce to four logical devices: three groups of fingers plus one device that shares a gate but has a different L and stays separate. Merging is grouping by a key (type, gate, unordered source/drain pair, L), which is a hash-table pass over the devices. Without it, a four-finger layout would never match a single schematic device.

## The merged device's width

Once grouped, the merged device carries $W = \sum_i W_i$ over its fingers, and its L is the common L. Fingers of 200, 310 and 150 nm give W = 660 nm. The schematic often states $W$ per finger and a finger count instead; the tool must compare like with like, either total W or W per finger and count, as the deck's property rules say. Source and drain interchangeability matters: a finger with source and drain swapped is still parallel.

## Resistors and property tolerance

A layout resistor's value comes from its geometry: $R = R_s \sum_i L_i / W_i$, the sheet resistance times the number of squares, plus contact and bend corrections the deck defines. A poly resistor with $R_s = 200$ ohm per square drawn as segments 12 by 1 and 8 by 0.5 um has $12 + 16 = 28$ squares, so 5600 ohm. Against a schematic value of 5400 ohm, the difference is 3.7 percent. LVS reports a property error when the difference exceeds the deck's tolerance. Property checks run after topology matches, because only matched devices can be compared.

label: LVS as graph matching
lesson:
# LVS as graph matching

LVS asks whether the layout netlist and the schematic netlist describe the same circuit. Both are graphs of devices and nets, so the question is graph isomorphism with labels: device types, terminal kinds and properties. General isomorphism has no known polynomial algorithm, but circuit graphs are strongly labelled, and practical matchers solve them in near-linear time by partition refinement.

## The device-net bipartite graph

Model a netlist as a bipartite graph: one vertex per device, one vertex per net, and one edge per device terminal (gate, source, drain; bulk is often a fourth). An inverter has 2 devices and 4 nets (A, Y, VDD, GND), so 6 vertices and 6 edges. A NOR2 has 4 devices and 6 nets (A, B, Y, the internal node, VDD, GND): 10 vertices and 12 edges. Edges carry the terminal kind, and source and drain share one kind because they are interchangeable. This graph is the same structure as the netlist hypergraph, with each net expanded into a vertex.

## Isomorphism and invariants

Two netlists match if a bijection maps devices to devices of the same type and nets to nets so that every terminal edge is preserved with its label. Any isomorphism preserves invariants: device counts per type, the number of nets of each degree, and so on. If the layout has four nets with three terminals and the schematic five, they cannot match. Invariants prove mismatches cheaply but never prove a match. Refinement uses increasingly fine invariants, local neighbourhood signatures, to split vertices into classes that must map onto each other.

## From mismatch to diagnosis

A matcher refines both netlists together with shared colours, so each class can be compared across graphs. Classes with equal sizes are matched or ambiguous; a class with three layout nets but two schematic nets proves an error and points to where it is. Because colours depend on neighbourhoods, one short perturbs everything within a few hops, and the report can list hundreds of unmatched nets. Tools seed the partition with matched port names to anchor it, compare hierarchically by black-boxing verified cells, and report the first conflicting classes so a designer can find the root cause.

## Going deeper

Ebeling, "GeminiII: A Second Generation Layout Validation Program" (ICCAD, 1988); the Netgen documentation.

label: Partition refinement in netlist comparison
lesson:
# Partition refinement in netlist comparison

Partition refinement is the algorithm at the heart of LVS tools such as Netgen and Gemini. It colours every device and net, then repeatedly recolours each vertex by its own colour and the colours of its neighbours, until no class splits. Vertices left alone in a class are matched; classes that differ between the two netlists localize errors. Running it by hand on a small netlist shows exactly how information flows.

## One round of refinement

Start with devices coloured by type, VDD and GND in classes of their own (matched by name), and other nets coloured by degree. In a NOR2 (PMOS A from VDD to n1, PMOS B from n1 to Y, NMOS A and B from GND to Y), the initial classes are PMOS, NMOS, VDD, GND, the degree-2 nets {A, B, n1} and the degree-3 net Y: 6 classes. One round recolours each vertex by (its colour, the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour)). The two PMOS split (one touches VDD, one touches Y), and n1 splits from A and B (it touches source/drain, they touch gates): 8 classes.

## Rounds until stable

Refinement repeats until a round leaves the number of classes unchanged. In the NOR2, round two splits A from B, because A gates the PMOS next to VDD and B the PMOS next to Y. Round three splits the two NMOS, which differ only in their gate nets. Round four changes nothing, so the class counts are 6, 8, 9, 10 and there are three splitting rounds. Each round costs time linear in the number of edges, using hashing of signatures, and the number of rounds is bounded by the number of vertices but is small for real circuits because information spreads one hop per round.

## The stable partition

The stable partition is the coarsest partition in which vertices of the same class have the same number of neighbours of each class along each terminal kind. In the NOR2 every vertex ends in its own class: 10 singletons, so every device and net is matched. In general, singleton classes in both netlists match outright, equal-size larger classes are ambiguities resolved by tie-breaking, and unequal classes are errors. The procedure is colour refinement, the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, run on both graphs with shared colour names.

## Going deeper

Ebeling, "GeminiII: A Second Generation Layout Validation Program" (ICCAD, 1988); the Netgen documentation.

label: Symmetry and ambiguity in LVS matching
lesson:
# Symmetry and ambiguity in LVS matching

Refinement cannot separate vertices that are truly symmetric: two identical inverters with private inputs and outputs look the same from every angle. LVS tools then break ties by choice and refine again. Understanding when refinement stalls, why a choice is safe, and when it is not explains both the speed of LVS and its rare pathological cases.

## Classes refinement cannot split

If an automorphism of the graph maps vertex $u$ to $v$, refinement always gives them the same colour, because every signature is preserved. Three identical NAND2 gates with private inputs and outputs, with only VDD and GND named, stabilize with 10 classes: VDD, GND, and eight classes of size three (four device roles and four net roles, one vertex per gate in each). Eight classes still contain more than one vertex. Such ties are not errors: equal-size classes in both netlists mean the matcher needs more information or an arbitrary choice.

## Breaking ties

When refinement stalls, the matcher picks one layout vertex and one schematic vertex from the same ambiguous class, gives them a fresh unique colour, and refines again. The new colour propagates and usually resolves everything connected to it. For $k$ identical independent gates, $k - 1$ choices suffice: after pairing all but one, the last is forced. If the tied vertices are truly symmetric, any choice works, because an automorphism maps one choice onto another. If they are only indistinguishable to refinement but not symmetric, as in some highly regular graphs, a wrong choice leads to a contradiction and must be undone.

## Names, permutations and regular arrays

Port and label names are the cheapest symmetry breakers: each pre-matched net gets a unique colour, and the inverters attached to it separate at once. Names can also create mismatches: if NAND2 inputs A and B are named and the layout swaps which one drives the bottom transistor of the stack, a transistor-level comparison reports a mismatch although the logic is the same, unless the tool is told those inputs may be permuted. Memory arrays are the hardest case, with millions of truly symmetric bit cells, which is why LVS flows name word and bit lines or compare the bit cell hierarchically.

In each round, every vertex gets a new colour made of its current colour plus the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour) over its edges, where the terminal kinds are gate and source/drain (source and drain are interchangeable). Refinement runs until the number of classes stops changing. Only VDD and GND are matched by name; no other port names are used. How many classes of the stable partition still contain more than one vertex?

A) 5

B) 0

C) 8

D) 14
problems.e: Identical gates with private inputs and outputs are automorphic images of each other, so refinement can never separate them. The stable partition has 14 classes, 8 of them with more than one member; the matcher must break each tie by an arbitrary choice and refine again.

A) Pick one layout and one schematic vertex from a class, pair them with a fresh colour, and refine again

B) Stop and report the netlists as equivalent

C) Report a mismatch

D) Merge the two inverters into one device
problems.a: Pick one layout and one schematic vertex from a class, pair them with a fresh colour, and refine again
problems.e: An arbitrary pairing breaks the tie; the new unique colour then propagates and usually resolves everything connected to it.

problems.q:
Three identical inverters each have private input and output nets, and no names are used. How many arbitrary tie-breaks does the matcher need?

A) 2

B) 3

C) 1

D) 6
problems.e: After pairing one inverter's vertices, the other two are still tied; one more choice leaves the last one forced. k identical independent copies need k - 1 choices.

A) Because symmetric vertices always have the same name

B) Because refinement already proved them equal

C) An automorphism maps any one choice onto any other, so every choice leads to a valid match

D) Because the matcher tries every choice in parallel
problems.a: An automorphism maps any one choice onto any other, so every choice leads to a valid match
problems.e: True symmetry means the graph looks the same from each tied vertex, so committing to one does not lose a match.

B) The comparison becomes slower

C) The inverters merge into one device

D) The labels pre-match those nets, so refinement separates the two inverters without any tie-break
problems.a: The labels pre-match those nets, so refinement separates the two inverters without any tie-break
problems.e: Each named net gets its own colour; its neighbours then differ, and the symmetry is gone.

B) Yes, every class must be a singleton

C) Yes, it proves a short

problems.a: Not by itself: equal sizes mean an ambiguity to resolve by a tie-break
problems.e: Only unequal sizes prove a mismatch. Equal-size classes need a choice, after which refinement continues.

label: Diagnosing LVS errors
lesson:
# Diagnosing LVS errors

An LVS report is a list of symptoms: unmatched nets, unmatched devices, property errors. Each class of physical mistake leaves a typical signature, and one mistake can produce hundreds of symptoms. Tool designers shape reports around these signatures, and designers and agents fix the root cause, not the symptoms.

## Shorts and opens

A short merges two nets: two different label names land on one extracted net, and devices of both schematic nets attach to it. An open splits a net: one schematic net matches two layout nets, each with part of the connections, typically because of a missing via, a gap, or a crossing without a via. A label placed on a text layer that does not attach to the pin's metal names nothing, so the port appears missing. These are connectivity errors, and they change the graph that refinement works on.

## Device and property errors

When the topology matches but devices differ, the report shows device-level errors. A W of 400 nm against 450 nm with a 5 percent tolerance is a property error. A missing implant changes the recognized device type. Fingers that are not merged, because parallel reduction is off or the fingers differ in L, give a device-count mismatch. A PMOS whose well is tied to the wrong supply mismatches on its bulk terminal. These errors are local to the device and do not cascade, unlike shorts and opens.

## Debugging order

Fix shorts first, then opens, then device and property errors, rerunning after each step. A single short perturbs refinement around it and can produce dozens of unmatched nets that disappear once it is fixed. Short finders locate a short by a shortest path through the merged net's shapes between a point labelled with one name and a point labelled with the other. When a clean block suddenly fails with hundreds of errors after a small edit, suspect one connectivity change. Hard IP without a netlist is black-boxed: only its pins are compared.

A) LVS does not check metal 1

B) The wires are on the wrong net names

C) The extractor ignores metal 2

D) Crossing metals connect only through a via; none was drawn
problems.a: Crossing metals connect only through a via; none was drawn
problems.e: Extraction follows the deck's connect statements: same-layer overlap and vias. A crossing alone is not a connection.

C) The label is moved to metal 1 automatically

D) A short is reported
problems.a: The label does not attach to the shape, so the port is reported as missing or unconnected
problems.e: Labels attach only to shapes on the layer the deck associates with that text layer. Misplaced text leaves the net unnamed.

problems.a: A device-type mismatch or a missing device, because recognition depends on the implant layer
problems.e: Device recognition is a Boolean expression of layers. Remove one layer and the device is recognized as something else, or not at all.

label: Electrical rule checking
lesson:
# Electrical rule checking

Electrical rule checks look for circuits that are connected as drawn but electrically wrong: floating gates, untapped wells, two drivers on one net, devices exposed to voltages beyond their rating. They run on the extracted netlist, often together with LVS, and they catch mistakes that a schematic comparison cannot, because the schematic may contain the same mistake.

## Floating gates

A gate net is floating if it reaches only gate terminals and is not a port of the cell: nothing drives it. In a netlist of an inverter, a NAND2 and a NOR2 whose inputs are A to E, any input net not declared as a port is floating. A floating gate settles at an undefined voltage and can leave both transistors of a stage partly on, burning static current. The check is a pass over nets: collect each net's terminal kinds, then flag nets with only gate terminals and no port or driver.

## Well taps

Every n-well must be tied to its supply through an n-plus tap, and the substrate tied to ground through p-plus taps. An untapped well floats, which shifts the PMOS thresholds through the body effect and raises the risk of latch-up, the parasitic thyristor formed by the n-well and substrate. The ERC check tests, for each well region, whether at least one tap lies inside it; a stricter rule bounds the distance from any transistor to the nearest tap. Standard-cell rows usually rely on tap cells placed at a fixed pitch, so a missing tap cell shows up here.

## Other electrical rules

Further ERC checks include multiple drivers on one net (contention), gates tied directly to a supply rather than through tie-high or tie-low cells (oxide stress), signals crossing between power domains without a level shifter, thin-oxide devices connected to high-voltage nets, and dangling nets that connect to a single terminal. Voltage-aware checks propagate the possible voltage of each net from the supplies and compare it with each device's rating. ERC findings are often warnings rather than errors, and decks distinguish the two so that signoff is not blocked by benign cases.

label: Antenna rules
lesson:
# Antenna rules

During manufacturing, plasma etching of each metal layer charges the exposed metal. If that metal is connected to a transistor gate and to no diffusion that can drain the charge, the charge flows through the thin gate oxide and can damage it. Antenna rules bound the ratio of collecting area to gate area. The check needs connectivity at an intermediate process step, which makes it unlike any purely geometric rule.

## The area antenna ratio

The area ratio is the area of metal connected to a gate, divided by the total gate area on that net. All gates on the net share the collected charge, so their areas add. A net with metal 2 pieces of 24 by 0.14 um and 40 by 0.2 um (3.36 and 8 square um) connected to one gate with W = 0.42 um and L = 0.13 um (0.0546 square um) has a ratio of $11.36 / 0.0546 = 208.1$. Gate area is W times L of the channel. Metal that also touches a source or drain diffusion is protected, because the junction leaks the charge away, which is the basis of the diode fix.

## The longest safe wire

Inverting the ratio gives the longest wire a router may run on one layer before it needs a fix. For a ratio limit $R$, gate area $G$ and wire width $w$, the length must satisfy $w L / G \le R$, so $L \le R G / w$. With $R = 850$, $G = 0.495$ square um and $w = 0.4$ um, $L \le 1051.9$ um, so 1051 um. Routers use this bound to plan layer changes before they create a violation, which is cheaper than repairing afterwards. A larger fanout raises $G$ and relaxes the bound.

## Side-wall ratios

For thick metal layers, charge collects through the side walls exposed during etch, so decks measure the side-wall area: the perimeter of the connected metal times the layer thickness. A 44 by 0.2 um wire, 0.5 um thick, has perimeter $2(44 + 0.2) = 88.4$ um and side-wall area 44.2 square um; on a gate of 0.26 square um the ratio is 170. Decks may also bound via-cut area ratios separately. Each layer can carry its own limit and measurement mode, so an antenna engine evaluates a small formula per layer per net rather than one global number.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference, sections on antenna properties; the OpenROAD documentation for antenna checking and repair.

label: Partial and cumulative antenna ratios
lesson:
# Partial and cumulative antenna ratios

Antenna damage happens layer by layer. When metal $i$ is etched, the layers above it do not yet exist, so only metal connected to the gate through layers 1 to $i$ is electrically attached. Antenna checks therefore compute a partial ratio for each layer and, in many decks, a cumulative ratio that adds them. Getting the process-step connectivity right is the core of an antenna engine.

## Partial ratios

The partial ratio of layer $i$ counts only the layer-$i$ metal already connected to the gate when layer $i$ is etched: connected through layers 1 to $i$. Consider a gate of 0.36 square um with 58 square um of metal 2 reaching it through metal 1 and metal 2, and another 69 square um of metal 2 that reaches it only through metal 4. When metal 2 is etched, the second piece is floating, so the metal 2 partial ratio is $58 / 0.36 = 161.1$, not $127 / 0.36$. The engine computes, per layer, the connectivity of the stack truncated at that layer.

## Cumulative ratios

Charge damage accumulates over steps, so many decks also bound a cumulative ratio: at layer $i$, the sum of the partial ratios of layers 1 to $i$. With partial areas 17, 3, 36 and 41 square um on metals 1 to 4 and a gate of 0.07 square um, the cumulative ratio at metal 4 is $97 / 0.07 = 1385.7$. Metal that joins the gate only through a higher layer never counts in its own layer's partial ratio, so it never enters the sum. This is why breaking a long lower-layer wire with an upper-layer jumper works.

## The worst layer

Each layer has its own limit, often different for thin and thick metals, and the deck checks every one. The worst layer is the one with the largest partial ratio relative to its limit. A net with partial areas 32, 56, 8 and 36 square um on a 0.27 square um gate peaks at metal 2 with 207.4. A repair should target that layer: moving metal 2 length to a higher layer, or adding a diode that protects all layers at once. An antenna engine reports the violating layer so the router can choose the fix.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference, sections on ANTENNAPARTIALMETALAREA and the cumulative antenna ratios.

label: Antenna diodes
lesson:
# Antenna diodes

The standard antenna fix is a reverse-biased diode on the gate's net: a small diffusion region that leaks the plasma charge to the substrate before it can stress the oxide. Diodes are cheap in area but add capacitance and leakage to the net. Routers insert them from a library diode cell, and decks state how much protection a given diode area buys.

## Removing excess metal

Without protection, the metal on the net must satisfy $M \le R_0 G$, where $R_0$ is the limit and $G$ the gate area. A net with 74.6 square um of metal 3 on a 0.15 square um gate, with $R_0 = 250$, may keep 37.5 square um, so 37.1 square um must leave metal 3. In practice the metal is not deleted: the route moves to another layer or is broken by a jumper so that the excess is not connected when metal 3 is etched. The excess quantifies how hard the violation is and which fix can absorb it.

## Sizing the diode protection

Decks state the allowed ratio as a function of the diode (diffusion) area attached to the net, often as a piecewise-linear table. On a linear segment, the limit rises from $R_0$ by $k$ per square um of diode. With a ratio of 742.8 against $R_0 = 300$ and $k = 600$, the net needs 0.738 square um of diode; with diode cells of 0.25 square um, $\lceil 442.8 / 150 \rceil = 3$ cells. Real tables saturate, so very large violations may need a jumper instead. Each diode adds junction capacitance and leakage, a small timing and power cost that the flow must re-extract.

## Diodes on nets with several gates

One diode protects every gate on the net, because they share one node: the charge leaks through the diode regardless of which gate it would have reached. With several gates, the ratio uses their summed area, which already lowers it. Four gates totalling 0.905 square um with 443.5 square um of metal give a ratio of 490.1; with $R_0 = 400$ and 20 per diode cell, 5 cells are needed. Placement matters only electrically, not geometrically, so routers put the diode near a convenient gate or at the driver, and engines verify by recomputing the net's ratio with the diode area included.

label: Layer jumpers and antenna repair
lesson:
# Layer jumpers and antenna repair

A layer jumper breaks a long lower-layer route near the gate and carries it over a higher layer. When the lower layer is etched, only the short stub is connected to the gate, so the partial ratio collapses. Jumpers cost two vias and a little upper-layer routing; diodes cost area and capacitance. Antenna repair in a router, such as OpenROAD's repair step, chooses between them per net.

## How a jump cuts the antenna

A metal 1 route 661 um long and 0.14 um wide on a 0.15 square um gate has a ratio of 616.9. If the router jumps to metal 2 at 28 um from the gate and returns to metal 1 only at the far end, then when metal 1 is etched the far piece is not yet connected (it joins only through metal 2), and the gate sees $0.14 \cdot 28 / 0.15 = 26.1$. The metal 2 jumper is short and adds little to the metal 2 partial ratio. The fix uses exactly the process-step connectivity that partial ratios model.

## Where to jump

The jump must happen close enough to the gate that the stub, plus any pin shape, stays within the limit: $(A_{pin} + w s) / G \le R$, so $s \le (R G - A_{pin}) / w$. With $G = 0.065$ square um, a 0.6 square um pin, $w = 0.28$ um and $R = 600$, $s \le 137.1$ um, so the router may run 137 um on metal 1 before jumping. Routers compute this distance during route planning and insert the via there, rather than discovering the violation later.

## Jump or diode

A jump moves the violating length up one layer, so it is impossible on the top layer, and it works only if the upper layer's own partial ratio stays within its limit after the addition. A net violating on metal 3 whose metal 4 partial ratio is 108 can take a jump adding 250 under a limit of 350, while a net violating on the top metal needs a diode. Repair engines try the cheaper fix first, check the result by recomputing ratios, and fall back to diodes. The decision is a small rule system, which makes it a natural Tier 1 policy for an agent to tune.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation for repair_antennas and the global router's antenna avoidance.

label: Metal fill and density
lesson:
# Metal fill and density

Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material at a rate that depends on the local pattern density: sparse regions dish, dense regions erode. Foundries therefore require the metal density of every window to lie between a minimum and a maximum. Density is a union area clipped to a window, computed over many windows, so a density engine is a Boolean and area engine organized around windows.

## Density of one window

The density of a window is the area of metal inside it divided by the window area. Shapes must be clipped to the window (AND), and overlapping shapes merged (OR), or overlaps are counted twice. In a $70 \times 70$ um window, a shape $[62, 80] \times [-8, 16]$ contributes only its clipped part $[62, 70] \times [0, 16]$, 128 square um. If the merged, clipped shapes total 1276 square um, the density is $1276 / 4900 = 26.0$ percent. A union-area sweep computes the merged area in $O(n \log n)$ for $n$ shapes.

## Checking a tiling of windows

A density rule is checked over many windows. With a $2 \times 2$ tiling of an $80 \times 80$ um region into $40 \times 40$ windows and a 25 percent minimum, each window's density is computed from its own clipped shapes, and a shape that spans two windows contributes to both. Densities of 30.6, 6.9, 12.5 and 40.1 percent mean two windows fail. Shapes near window boundaries are where off-by-one clipping errors appear, so engines clip with half-open intervals and test against a brute-force reference.

## Density from routing pitch

Regular structures give density directly. Parallel wires of width $w$ at pitch $p$ fill a fraction $w / p$ of the area they cover. A $170 \times 170$ um window with a $60 \times 20$ um blockage and the rest routed at 0.28 um width and 0.84 um pitch has density $(28900 - 1200)(1/3) / 28900 = 31.9$ percent. Such estimates let a floorplanner predict density problems before routing: large blockages, analog areas and pad rings are the usual low-density regions, and wide power straps the usual high-density ones.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Robins, Singh and Zelikovsky, "Filling algorithms and analyses for layout density control" (IEEE TCAD, 1999).

label: Fill insertion to a density target
lesson:
# Fill insertion to a density target

Fill tools add electrically inactive metal shapes to windows below the minimum density. The amount needed is simple arithmetic; where the fill may go is a geometric problem, because fill must keep spacing to existing metal and stay out of keep-out regions. A fill engine is a constrained placement of many small squares, followed by a density re-check.

## Fill needed for a target

If a window of area $A_w$ holds metal area $A_m$ and the minimum density is $D$, fill must add at least $D A_w - A_m$. With fill squares of side $f$ placed only in empty space, the count is $\lceil (D A_w - A_m) / f^2 \rceil$. A $130 \times 130$ um window with 3339 square um of metal and a 20 percent minimum needs $3380 - 3339 = 41$ square um, so two $5 \times 5$ squares. Real tools overshoot slightly to keep margin against the maximum density and against windows that overlap this one.

## Legal fill sites

Fill candidates sit on a grid, and a candidate is legal only if it keeps the fill spacing $s$ to all metal: the square grown by $s$ must not overlap any metal shape. Equivalently the free region is the window NOT (metal SIZED BY $s$), and a candidate is legal if it lies inside it. On a $28 \times 28$ um window with 2 um squares on a 4 um grid and 1 um spacing, 40 of 49 candidates may survive three metal shapes. Engines test candidates with a spatial index over the sized metal, or rasterize the free region.

## The best reachable density

Filling every legal site gives the largest density fill can reach: the existing metal plus the legal squares, over the window area. With 293 square um of metal and 24 legal squares of 9 square um in a 1764 square um window, the best is $509 / 1764 = 28.9$ percent. If that is still below the minimum, no fill solution exists, and the design must change: open a blockage, move a macro, or obtain a waiver. Checking this bound first prevents a fill engine from searching for a solution that cannot exist.

lesson:
# Sliding density windows and gradients

Density rules apply to windows that slide across the die with a fixed step, not to a fixed tiling. Some rules also bound how fast density may change between neighbouring windows. Efficient engines precompute per-tile areas once and assemble windows from tiles, which turns a quadratic amount of clipping into prefix-sum lookups.

## Counting window positions

A $w \times w$ window stepping by $t$ over a $D_x \times D_y$ die takes $(D_x - w)/t + 1$ positions in x and $(D_y - w)/t + 1$ in y. A 20 um window with a 20 um step over a 520 by 740 um die gives $26 \cdot 37 = 962$ positions; halving the step roughly quadruples the count. Each position needs a density, so computing each from scratch would clip the same shapes many times. The step is a rule parameter: a smaller step catches more local extremes.

## The minimum window by tile sums

Cut the die into tiles of the step size and compute each tile's metal area once with a union sweep. A window covering $k \times k$ tiles has area equal to the sum of its tiles, so its density is the mean of their densities. A two-dimensional prefix sum $P$ gives any window's sum as $P(i_2, j_2) - P(i_1, j_2) - P(i_2, j_1) + P(i_1, j_1)$ in constant time. On a $5 \times 5$ tile grid with $2 \times 2$ windows there are 16 positions; the minimum mean, say 20.8 percent, is the window a fill engine must fix first.

## Density gradients

Polishing also suffers when density changes sharply between nearby regions, so some decks bound the difference between windows one step apart. Neighbouring windows share most of their tiles, so their difference depends only on the tiles that enter and leave. With $2 \times 2$ windows over a $5 \times 5$ grid, there are 24 horizontal and vertical neighbour pairs; the largest absolute difference, for example 14.5 percentage points, is compared with the limit. A gradient violation is fixed by filling the sparse side or slotting the dense side, not by meeting the minimum alone.

lesson:
# Fill side effects and fill-aware flows

Fill is metal, so it changes capacitance, and it lives in the same layout as signal wiring, so it must be removed and regenerated when routing changes. Fill-aware flows control where fill goes, how it is tied, and when it is inserted relative to extraction and timing signoff. Ignoring these effects is a common way to fail timing after a clean DRC.

## Coupling added by fill

A first-order sidewall model makes each side's coupling capacitance proportional to the run length and thickness over the spacing, $C \propto t L / s$. A wire with a neighbour at 170 nm on one side and nothing on the other gains, when fill lands 40 nm away on the empty side, a new term proportional to $1/40$, which is $170 / 40 = 425$ percent of the original sidewall term. Real extraction is three-dimensional and fill is often floating, so the actual increase is smaller, but the model shows why fill near critical nets must be controlled.

## Timing-aware and grounded fill

Timing-aware fill keeps a larger spacing from critical nets, or keeps fill out of their neighbourhood, and makes up density elsewhere in the window. Fill can be floating or tied to a supply. Grounded fill adds a definite capacitance to ground; floating fill couples the nets around it through a conductor of unknown potential, which extraction tools must model specially. Keep-out regions protect analog and RF nets. After fill, signoff timing must use parasitics extracted with the fill present.

## Where fill lives in the flow

Fill is inserted after detailed routing, when the gaps are known, and before final extraction, DRC and timing signoff. Front-end layers (poly, diffusion) get dummy fill too, for polishing and etch uniformity. Wide metal that exceeds the maximum density is slotted. When an ECO changes routing, fill near the change is stripped and regenerated, then re-extracted. Open-source flows insert fill with OpenROAD's density fill or KLayout scripts, and commercial flows offer timing-aware fill modes.

label: Lithography hotspot detection
lesson:
# Lithography hotspot detection

Design rules are a simplified contract with lithography. Some rule-clean patterns still print badly: lines pinch, spaces bridge, line ends pull back, especially at the edges of the process window. Hotspot detection finds these patterns before tape-out, using pattern libraries, learned classifiers and lithography simulation. It is the clearest case in physical verification of a fast screen backed by an accurate engine.

## Precision and recall of a detector

A detector is judged against ground truth from lithography simulation. If it flags 56 true hotspots and 286 clean clips and misses 28 hotspots, its recall is $56 / 84 = 66.7$ percent and its precision $56 / 342 = 16.4$ percent. Recall measures how many real hotspots are caught; every miss is potential yield loss. Precision measures how many flags are real; every false alarm costs simulation time or an unnecessary layout change. Signoff flows require very high recall and buy precision with confirmatory simulation.

## What makes a hotspot

A hotspot is a pattern that fails to print within tolerance somewhere in the process window, the range of focus and exposure dose the fab expects. Typical failures are pinching (a line narrows), bridging (a space closes) and line-end shortening. Printing depends on all geometry within the optical interaction range, so the same pattern can be safe in one neighbourhood and a hotspot in another: a hotspot is a pattern together with its context. OPC corrects most proximity effects; hotspots are what remains difficult after correction.

## Detection methods

Full-chip lithography simulation is the most accurate and the slowest: it computes the aerial image and resist response everywhere. Pattern matching looks up known bad patterns exactly or with tolerances; it is fast and precise but blind to new patterns. Machine-learning classifiers generalize to unseen clips but make false alarms and misses, so their flags are confirmed by simulation. Fixes change geometry where there is room: wire spreading, widening, or rerouting with a hotspot cost. Pattern libraries from foundries are confidential, which shapes how detectors are deployed.

## Going deeper

The ICCAD 2012 CAD contest on fuzzy pattern matching for physical verification; the "Handbook of Algorithms for Physical Design Automation" (Alpert, Mehta and Sapatnekar, eds.), chapters on lithography and DFM.

label: Pattern matching for DFM
lesson:
# Pattern matching for DFM

Pattern matching scans a layout for every occurrence of a known problematic pattern. Patterns come from foundry libraries, from earlier hotspots, or from failure analysis. On a rasterized clip, matching is a sliding-window comparison; production engines hash windows and use topological signatures so that a full chip is searched in one pass. Rotations, mirrors and don't-care regions make one pattern cover a family of layouts.

## Exact matching of a raster pattern

Rasterize the layer into pixels (1 for metal) and slide a $p \times q$ pattern over every position of an $R \times C$ grid: there are $(R - p + 1)(C - q + 1)$ positions, and a match requires every pixel to agree. A $2 \times 2$ pattern over a $5 \times 5$ grid has 16 positions. Production matchers avoid pixel-by-pixel comparison by hashing each window (rolling hashes update in constant time as the window slides), or by encoding a clip's edge topology and dimensions so that matches survive small shifts.

## Orientation-invariant matching

Lithography treats a pattern and its rotations alike (for symmetric illumination), so a library entry should match in all orientations. The matcher generates the rotated versions (90, 180, 270 degrees; mirrors add four more) and counts positions where at least one matches. A position is counted once even if several orientations match it. A $2 \times 2$ pattern 10, 10 matches twice unrotated in a grid but eight times with rotations. Hash-based matchers store the canonical form of each pattern, the smallest hash over its orientations, so one lookup covers all of them.

## Don't-care pixels

Fuzzy patterns mark some pixels as don't-care, matching either value, so one entry covers every layout that agrees on the constrained pixels. A $3 \times 3$ pattern with three don't-cares compares six pixels per position. More don't-cares mean more matches, both real hotspots and false alarms. Library designers trade coverage against precision; learned detectors can be seen as a soft version of the same idea, where the model decides which pixels matter.

## Going deeper

The ICCAD 2012 CAD contest on fuzzy pattern matching for physical verification.

label: Double-patterning coloring conflicts
lesson:
# Double-patterning coloring conflicts

When features are packed tighter than one exposure can print, double patterning splits a layer onto two masks. Two features closer than the same-mask spacing must go on different masks, which makes mask assignment a graph 2-coloring problem. A layout is decomposable exactly when its conflict graph is bipartite, so double-patterning checks reduce to finding odd cycles.

## Building the conflict graph

Each feature is a vertex, and an edge joins two features closer than the same-mask spacing $S$, measured as Euclidean distance. With $S = 27$ nm, five features may produce two edges. Building the graph is a spacing check with a larger distance: candidate pairs from a sweep, then exact distances. Edges mean must-differ constraints. Features farther than $S$ from everything form isolated vertices, free to go on either mask, which the decomposer uses to balance density between the masks.

## Odd cycles

A graph is 2-colourable if and only if it has no odd cycle. A breadth-first search that alternates colours finds a same-colour edge exactly in a component that contains an odd cycle. Three features each closer than $S$ to the other two form a triangle, which no assignment can satisfy. Each component is checked separately, and each non-bipartite component is a double-patterning violation. Fixes are a layout change that removes an edge, or a stitch that splits one feature into two overlapping parts on different masks, where the process allows stitches.

## Counting mask assignments

A connected bipartite component has exactly two colourings: fix one vertex's mask and every other vertex is forced. Components are independent, so a graph with $c$ components, all bipartite, has $2^c$ assignments, counting isolated features as components; one odd component makes the count zero. Seven features in two components give 4 assignments. Decomposers use this freedom to balance pattern density between masks and to avoid stitches. Triple patterning raises the problem to 3-coloring, which is NP-complete in general, and changes the algorithms used.

label: Critical area of a layout
lesson:
# Critical area of a layout

Random particle defects cause shorts and opens. Whether a defect of a given size kills the chip depends on where it lands: the critical area is the area of positions where its centre causes a failure. Averaged over the defect size distribution and multiplied by defect density, it predicts yield. Critical-area analysis turns layout geometry into a yield number and drives DFM fixes such as wire spreading.

## Critical area at one defect size

For two long parallel wires with gap $s$ and run length $L$, a circular conducting defect of diameter $x$ shorts them when it touches both. For $x \le s$ that is impossible; for $x > s$ its centre must fall in a band of width $x - s$ between the wires, so $A_c(x) = L (x - s)$, ignoring end effects. With $L = 150$ um, $s = 135$ nm and $x = 220$ nm, the band is 85 nm wide and $A_c = 12.75$ square um. Opens are the dual: a missing-material defect of diameter $x$ cuts a wire of width $w$ when $x > w$, with $A_c = L(x - w)$.

## Averaging over defect sizes

Defect sizes follow a distribution, commonly $f(x) = 2 x_0^2 / x^3$ for $x \ge x_0$. The average short critical area of one gap is $\int_s^\infty L (x - s) f(x)\, dx = L x_0^2 / s$ for $s \ge x_0$. A bus of 4 wires has 3 gaps; with $L = 470$ um, $x_0 = 25$ nm and $s = 75$ nm the average is $3 \cdot 470 \cdot 625 / 75 / 1000 = 11.75$ square um, counting each gap separately. The $1 / s$ dependence explains why widening gaps pays off most where they are smallest.

## From critical area to yield

With defect density $D$ for a mechanism and average critical area $A_c$, the Poisson model gives yield $Y = e^{-D A_c}$. Units must agree: 13.3 square mm is 0.133 square cm, so with $D = 0.39$ defects per square cm, $D A_c = 0.05187$ and $Y = 94.95$ percent. Yields of independent mechanisms and layers multiply, so a chip's random-defect yield is the product over layers of shorts and opens. Clustered defects are modelled with negative binomial yield instead. Critical area is computed by Boolean and sizing operations, so it runs in the same engines as DRC.

## Going deeper

Stapper, "Modeling of integrated circuit defect sensitivities" (IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1983).
